doc.title: Urbie Green interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: Best recordings: playing as sideman versus leader
summary: Says he played better on others' records; recalls spots with Tony Bennett and Billie Holiday's Lady in Satin.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her

blocks.x: If you had, if you could pick out a record or two that you would want people to identify as one of your best, was there a time or a particular record or recording that you are most happy with?
Yeah, uh, I think maybe I played better on other people’s records than I played on my own. I’m not sure.
Well there’s less to worry about, right?

Yeah as a player. When you’re the leader you’ve got all these headaches and you’re worrying about the other guys showing up, and how much money you’re costing the record company, and if we go overtime I’ll never record with them again. And all kinds of things when you’re the leader you know. I don’t know. There was a record I did with Tony Bennett a long time ago. I had a couple of spots on it that I got into some kind of other frame of mind for a few bars. It was something about New York My Home Town or something like that. And he did some kind of eerie songs, not really eerie, but anyway like “Lonesome in the City” and that kinds of bluesy feel of Manhattan. And I think I made a few wolf calls or something, you know on a ballad. And I did a thing with Billie Holiday that had a couple of nice spots there that I felt pretty good about — “Lady in Satin” album. That was all ballads I think. Tony and I did the “Penthouse Serenade” where I started way out low like a bass trombone for a while. It came out better than I thought it would.
